sentence: Ten-year-old male, with no personal history of interest, who went to the Emergency Department of the Primary Care center with a four-hour history of abdominal pain, fever of 40 °C, food vomiting and diarrhea with traces of mucus.
Abdominal examination reveals diffuse abdominal pain, somewhat more in the right iliac fossa, with signs of peritoneal irritation.
The analysis shows 12,200 leukocytes/µl (91% neutrophils) and a slight elevation of C-reactive protein (CRP).
He is referred to the nearest hospital with the suspicion of an acute abdomen to complete the study.
An abdominal ultrasound was performed, showing a tubular, aperistaltic and incompressible image with the transducer, compatible with acute appendicitis.

It was decided to perform a surgical intervention, after receiving informed consent from the parents, and an appendectomy was carried out during which a cecal appendix with mild inflammatory signs was observed.
The postoperative course was torpid, with persistent fever (38.8 °C), generalized abdominal pain without peritonism, vomiting and diarrhea.
An abdominal ultrasound was performed, which reported dilation of the loops of the small intestine, which suggests an incomplete obstructive condition.
Laboratory tests continue to show leukocytosis with a left shift and elevated C-reactive protein.

Given the inconsistency of the patient's symptoms and the surgical findings, it was decided to opt for conservative treatment, performing a stool culture, and empirical antibiotic therapy was started while awaiting the results of the stool culture, which reported Campylobacter jejuni sensitive to gentamicin.

Antibiotic treatment with gentamicin was started, with which the patient's evolution was satisfactory, as the clinical condition resolved and the patient was discharged ten days after the surgical intervention.
The pathological study of the cecal appendix was reported as cecal appendix with inflammatory signs.
